title: Talking to Your Computer: The Terminal

intro.text: As a manager of an AI coding assistant, you won't write the code — but you will need to work in the place where the AI actually operates: the terminal. It's where you'll launch Claude Code, watch what it does, and run the quick checks that tell you whether the work was done right. This chapter takes you from “what is that black window?” to confidently creating, exploring, and verifying folders from the command line on your own machine.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: Lessons 1.2 and 1.3 cover the same skills on different operating systems. Work through the one that matches your laptop — you only need one of them. Commands differ slightly between Windows and macOS, so follow the lesson for your OS.

lessons.title: The CLI and the Terminal
lessons.objective: Understand GUI, CLI, and the terminal so you can use and supervise an AI coding agent.

steps.title: There are two ways to use a computer

blocks.text: Today we mostly control computers through a graphical screen: right-click to make a new folder, double-click to open it, drag a file to move it. It feels so natural that we forget it isn't the only way to talk to a computer.
GUI (Graphical User Interface)

That familiar way of working. You click icons you can see on the screen and drag files into folders — a graphics-based interface. Because you operate the computer with a mouse and graphics, it's called a Graphical User Interface — GUI for short. You just press what you see, so it's intuitive: anyone can pick it up in minutes.

blocks.alt: A graphical interface uses windows, icons, and buttons.
blocks.caption: A graphical interface uses windows, icons, and buttons.

blocks.text: Point, click, and drag what you can see — that's a GUI (Graphical User Interface).
CLI (Command Line Interface)

The complete opposite. Almost no mouse, almost no graphics. A dark window with a blinking cursor, where you type commands on the keyboard to make the computer do things. Because you drive the computer with lines of commands, it's called a Command Line Interface — CLI for short.

blocks.alt: A text-based interface receives typed commands.
blocks.caption: A text-based interface receives typed commands.

blocks.text: Typing commands to talk to the computer — that's the CLI (Command Line Interface).

“Who still types commands in this day and age?” you might wonder. But the CLI is alive and well — it's still the main way developers work. Think of it like ordering food: tapping through the menu on a McDonald's self-order kiosk is the GUI; walking up to the counter and telling the cashier exactly what you want is the CLI.
“Almost every developer tool you'll use in this course — including Claude Code — runs in the CLI.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: That's why anyone managing AI-built software needs to be comfortable with the basics of the CLI. The AI does its work here, and this is where you'll watch it work, spot when something looks off, and run your own checks instead of taking the AI's word for it.
A terminal is simply the program that gives you a place to type those commands. It comes pre-installed on every computer — there's nothing to download.

blocks.title: How to open it on each computer

blocks.text: Opening the terminal on Windows
Click the Search box in the taskbar.
Type PowerShell.
Click Windows PowerShell to launch it.
Windows — search for PowerShell in the taskbar and run it.
Opening the terminal on macOS
Press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight.
Type terminal.
Press Enter to launch Terminal.

lessons.title: Terminal Basics — Windows
lessons.objective: Learn the core PowerShell commands well enough to verify with your own eyes what an AI assistant has created, moved, or deleted on Windows.

blocks.text: Open Start, type PowerShell, and select Windows PowerShell. Leave this window open for the next step.
The path in the prompt, such as C:\Users\yourname, is your current working directory. Commands run relative to this folder. Check it when you need to find files created by a command or by AI.
“A ‘directory’ is just another word for a folder.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: A PowerShell window is open, with a prompt showing your current folder.

blocks.title: Practice in a disposable folder
blocks.text: The commands below illustrate separate operations. After deleting test, create it again before trying cd test. Do not practice deletion on a folder containing work you need.
mkdir test
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for make directory. Creates a folder named test in your current location.
ls
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for list. Prints the files and folders in your current location — your quickest audit tool. When the AI says it created something, ls is how you see for yourself.
The list includes the test folder.

blocks.title: Remove only the empty test folder

blocks.text: rm test
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for remove. Deletes the file or folder you name.

blocks.title: Recreate test, then move between folders

blocks.text: Run the earlier mkdir test command again before continuing. Then run the following commands one at a time. Press Enter after each command and watch the path in the prompt.
cd test
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: cd ..
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: cd /
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for change directory.
. means the current folder; .. means the parent folder.
Type the first few letters of a folder name and press Tab — the terminal autocompletes it for you.
The top-level folder you can't go above is called the root folder.
clear
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Wipes the terminal output so you get a clean screen.
You created and removed an empty folder, changed directories, and cleared the display.

lessons.title: Terminal Basics — macOS
lessons.objective: Learn the core macOS Terminal commands well enough to verify with your own eyes what an AI assistant has created, moved, or deleted.

blocks.text: Press Command + Space, type Terminal, and press Return.
A Terminal window is open. Leave it open for this lesson.
To the left of the cursor you'll see something like yourname ~ %.
The ~ (tilde) is your home folder — your personal account folder, where Downloads, Documents, and friends live.
You type commands after the %.
pwd
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for print working directory. Prints the full path of the folder you're in right now — the first thing to check before judging any AI output, so you know you're inspecting the right project.
open .
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: The . means the current folder — this pops it open in Finder so you can see it the GUI way.
mkdir test
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: ls
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for make directory. Creates a folder in the current location. (Directory = folder.)
Prints the files and folders in the current location — your quickest way to confirm that what the AI says it made is actually there.

blocks.title: Reference: removing files and folders — do not run these examples

blocks.text: Delete:  rm

rm filename   # delete a file
rm -r foldername   # delete a folder AND everything inside it
rm -rf foldername   # force delete a folder AND everything inside it
blocks.label: Deletion examples

blocks.text: These examples permanently delete files or folders. Do not run them against a course project you want to keep.

blocks.title: Before you continue
blocks.text: rm -rf deletes instantly and permanently — nothing goes to the Trash. Double-check the folder name before you press Enter, and be extra alert whenever an AI assistant proposes running it.

blocks.title: Enter test, then return to its parent

blocks.text: Run these two commands one at a time.
cd test
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: cd ..
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Short for change directory. Type part of a folder name and press Tab to autocomplete.
clear
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Wipes the terminal output.
You found your current folder, opened it in Finder, created test, and moved into and out of it.

lessons.title: Terminal Shortcuts Worth Knowing
lessons.objective: Pick up the three keyboard shortcuts that make working in the terminal fast: recalling the previous command, wiping a mistyped line, and deleting word by word.

blocks.text: Press the up-arrow key (↑) and the command you just ran is pulled right back onto the line, ready to run or edit.
P.S. Extremely handy when you need to run the same command several times in a row — like re-running a version check after a fix.
Typed something wrong and want a clean start? One keystroke wipes everything you've entered:
Windows: ESC
macOS: Ctrl + U
If you'd rather delete what you typed one word at a time instead of all at once:
Windows: Ctrl + Backspace
macOS: Option + Backspace
